chapters.name: Chapter 1: Define and measure the problem

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Quality, Six Sigma and the five DMAIC steps
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name the five DMAIC steps and say what a Yellow Belt does in each.
This lesson builds toward: Given a description of an improvement project, you will name the five DMAIC steps in order and say what happens in each, with all five correct.
Quality means giving the customer what they need, the same way, every time. A defect is anything the customer would not accept: a wrong order, a late delivery, a missing part, a billing error.
Six Sigma is a method for cutting defects by using data instead of guesses. Lean is a method for cutting waste, the steps that add time but no value. Many employers teach them together as Lean Six Sigma.
Projects follow five steps called DMAIC: Define the problem, Measure how big it is, Analyze to find the root cause, Improve by testing a fix, and Control to keep the gain. Belts show training level: a Yellow Belt knows the basics and helps on projects, often by collecting data and mapping steps; Green and Black Belts lead bigger projects.
Two well-known Yellow Belt credentials are the ASQ Certified Six Sigma Yellow Belt and the IASSC Certified Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt. This course prepares you; only the certifying body grants the credential.
Step by step:
- Define: what is the problem and the goal?
- Measure: how often does it happen now?
- Analyze: what is the root cause?
- Improve: what fix works when you test it?
- Control: how do you keep the gain?
Words to know:
- Defect: anything the customer would not accept, such as a wrong, late or broken item.
- Six Sigma: a method for cutting defects by using data; very high quality means about 3.4 defects per million chances.
- Lean: a method for removing steps that waste time or materials.
- DMAIC: Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control: the five steps of a Six Sigma project.
- Yellow Belt: a person trained in the basics who helps on improvement projects.
Official sources:
- ASQ: Certified Six Sigma Yellow Belt (requirements, exam and Body of Knowledge)
- IASSC: Certified Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt (ICYB)
Try it now: Pick one process you know that goes wrong too often, at work, in a business or at home (for example orders sent late, lunch orders wrong, or invoices sent with errors). Write it at the top of a page, then write D, M, A, I, C down the side and one question you would ask in each step.
You can now name the five DMAIC steps in order, say what a Yellow Belt does, and pick a process to improve.

check.q: Which is the right order of the DMAIC steps?
check.why: DMAIC stands for Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control, in that order.

check.q: Your team is testing a new way to pack orders to see if errors drop. Which step is this?
check.why: Testing a fix to see whether it works happens in the Improve step.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Define: the problem statement and the process map
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a problem statement and goal, and draw a simple process map.
This lesson builds toward: Given a process that has a repeating problem, you will write a problem statement and a measurable goal and draw a simple process map, with what, where, when and how big, and no cause or solution in the statement.
A good project starts with a clear problem statement. It says what is wrong, where, since when and how big, and why it matters. It does NOT name a cause or a solution yet, because you have not found them. Example: "Since June, 12 of every 100 lunch orders at the downtown cafe go out wrong, causing refunds and complaints."
The goal says how much better, by when: "Cut wrong lunch orders to 3 of every 100 by the end of September."
Then map the process. Write each step in a box from start to finish and connect them with arrows. A SIPOC is a quick table of the big picture: Suppliers, Inputs, Process steps, Outputs and Customers. The voice of the customer (VOC) is what customers say they need; the parts that matter most to them are called critical to quality (CTQ).
Step by step:
- Write what is wrong, where, since when and how big.
- Add why it matters (cost, time, customers, safety).
- Check: no cause and no solution in the statement.
- Write a goal with a number and a date.
- Draw the process in 5 to 8 boxes, start to finish.
Words to know:
- Problem statement: a short, fact-based description of what is wrong, where, when and how big.
- Process map: a drawing of the steps of a process in order, using boxes and arrows.
- SIPOC: a one-page table of Suppliers, Inputs, Process, Outputs and Customers.
- Voice of the customer (VOC): what customers say they need or complain about.
- Critical to quality (CTQ): a feature that matters most to the customer, such as on time or correct.
Try it now: For the process you picked, write a problem statement with what, where, since when and how big (use your best estimate for now), a goal with a number and a date, and a process map of 5 to 8 boxes on paper.
You can now write a problem statement and goal, and draw a simple map of the process.

check.q: Which is the best problem statement?
options: "Since March, 8 of every 50 shipments from the east warehouse arrive late, causing customer refunds."
check.why: It gives what, where, since when and how big, and it does not blame a cause or name a solution.

check.q: What does the P in SIPOC stand for?
check.why: SIPOC is Suppliers, Inputs, Process, Outputs and Customers.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Measure: check sheets and defect rates
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Collect data on a check sheet and calculate a defect rate.
This lesson builds toward: Given a process to watch for one to two weeks, you will collect data on a check sheet and calculate a defect rate, with at least 20 data points and the math shown.
In the Measure step you find out how often the problem really happens. Guesses are often wrong, so you count.
A check sheet is a simple paper or spreadsheet form. Down the side, list the kinds of defects (wrong item, missing item, late). Across the top, list the days. Make a tally mark each time one happens, and also count the total units you checked.
The defect rate is defective units divided by total units, times 100. If 15 of 200 orders were wrong: 15 / 200 = 0.075, or 7.5%. Six Sigma also uses DPMO, defects per million opportunities: defects divided by (units times opportunities per unit), times 1,000,000. If 500 invoices each have 4 chances for an error and you find 10 errors: 10 / (500 x 4) = 0.005, times 1,000,000 = 5,000 DPMO.
Measure the same way every time: same definition of a defect, same time of day, same person or clear rules. This is your baseline, the "before" number you will compare with later.
Step by step:
- Write a clear definition of each defect.
- Make a check sheet: defect types down the side, days across the top.
- Tally each defect and count the total units checked.
- Defect rate = defective units / total units x 100.
- Record this as your baseline.
Words to know:
- Check sheet: a simple form for tallying how often each kind of problem happens.
- Defect rate: the share of units with a defect, shown as a percent.
- DPMO: defects per million opportunities: defects / (units x chances per unit) x 1,000,000.
- Baseline: how the process performs before you change it.
Try it now: Make a check sheet for your process on paper or in a spreadsheet. Collect at least 20 data points over the next week (start today), then calculate your defect rate and show the math. Practice now: 9 late of 150 deliveries is what percent? (Answer: 9 / 150 = 0.06 = 6%.)
You can now collect data on a check sheet, calculate a defect rate and set your baseline.

check.q: You checked 80 orders and 4 were wrong. What is the defect rate?
Why do you write one clear definition of each defect before counting?
options: So the boss can sign it
So everyone counts the same way and the numbers can be trusted
So you need fewer data points
check.why: If people count different things, the data cannot be compared or trusted.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Analyze: Pareto charts, fishbones and 5 Whys
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Find the biggest problem with a Pareto chart and its root cause with 5 Whys.
This lesson builds toward: Given your check-sheet data, you will find the biggest problem with a Pareto chart and dig to its root cause with 5 Whys, so the cause found is one the team can act on.
A Pareto chart is a bar chart sorted from the biggest bar to the smallest. It shows that a few causes usually make most of the problems, often called the 80/20 rule. Start with the biggest bar.
A fishbone diagram (also called a cause-and-effect or Ishikawa diagram) helps a team list possible causes. Write the problem at the "head", then draw bones for groups of causes, such as Methods, Machines, Materials, People, Measurement and Environment.
Then ask "Why?" about five times to dig from the symptom to a root cause you can fix. Example: Orders are wrong. Why? The cook misread the ticket. Why? The ticket was handwritten. Why? The printer is broken. Why? No one is in charge of fixing it. Why? There is no maintenance check. Root cause: no maintenance check on the printer.
Blame is not a root cause. If the answer is "someone was careless", keep asking why the process let the mistake happen.
Step by step:
- Total each defect type from your check sheet.
- Sort them biggest to smallest and draw the bars.
- Pick the biggest bar.
- List possible causes on a fishbone.
- Ask "Why?" about five times until you reach a cause you can act on.
Words to know:
- Pareto chart: a bar chart sorted from biggest to smallest, to show which few problems matter most.
- 80/20 rule: the pattern that a few causes often make most of the problems.
- Fishbone diagram: a drawing that groups possible causes of a problem; also called an Ishikawa diagram.
- Root cause: the real reason a problem happens; fix it and the problem stops or drops.
- 5 Whys: asking "Why?" again and again, about five times, to reach the root cause.
Try it now: Total each defect type from your check sheet, sort them and draw a Pareto chart on paper or in a spreadsheet. Then write a 5 Whys for the biggest bar. Stop when you reach a cause you can fix and that does not blame a person.
You can now draw a Pareto chart, pick the biggest problem and dig to its root cause with 5 Whys.

check.q: Your Pareto chart shows: wrong size 40, missing item 25, late 10, damaged 5. Where do you start?
options: All four at the same time
check.why: A Pareto chart tells you to start with the biggest bar, where a fix helps most.

check.q: Your 5 Whys ends at "the worker was careless". What should you do?
options: Stop there and write up the worker
Keep asking why the process let the mistake happen
Remove the worker from the chart
check.why: Blame is not a root cause; look for what in the process allowed the mistake.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Improve: remove waste and mistake-proof the work
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose a fix that removes waste or mistakes and test it on a small scale.
This lesson builds toward: Given a root cause, you will choose a fix that removes waste or mistakes, test it on a small scale and set up a control check, with data before and after the fix.
Lean names eight kinds of waste. An easy way to remember them is DOWNTIME: Defects, Overproduction, Waiting, Non-used talent, Transportation, Inventory (too much stock), Motion (extra walking or reaching) and Extra processing.
Good fixes often make the right way the easy way. 5S organizes a work area: Sort, Set in order, Shine, Standardize, Sustain. Mistake-proofing (poka-yoke in Japanese) makes errors hard or impossible, such as a plug that fits only one way, a form that will not submit with a blank box, or a color-coded bin.
Test the fix on a small scale first: one shift, one desk or one week. This is a pilot. Measure the same way as your baseline and compare. If the numbers got better, roll it out; if not, try the next idea.
Step by step:
- List fixes that attack the root cause.
- Prefer fixes that remove waste or make mistakes hard.
- Run a small pilot: one shift, one desk or one week.
- Measure the same way as the baseline.
- Compare before and after.
Words to know:
- Waste: any step that uses time or materials but adds no value for the customer.
- DOWNTIME: a memory aid for the eight wastes: Defects, Overproduction, Waiting, Non-used talent, Transportation, Inventory, Motion, Extra processing.
- 5S: Sort, Set in order, Shine, Standardize, Sustain: a way to organize a work area.
- Mistake-proofing (poka-yoke): a design that makes errors hard or impossible.
- Pilot: a small, short test of a fix before using it everywhere.
Try it now: Write three possible fixes for your root cause. Mark which waste each removes or how it mistake-proofs the work. Pick one, plan a small pilot (where, how long, who), and start measuring it the same way as your baseline.
You can now spot the eight wastes, choose a fix that removes waste or mistakes, and test it with a small pilot.

check.q: Workers walk across the warehouse many times a day to get tape. Which waste is this?
check.why: Extra walking and reaching by people is the waste of motion.

check.q: You have a fix you think will work. What is the best next step?
options: Test it on a small scale and compare with the baseline
Roll it out to every site at once
Skip measuring, since you are sure
check.why: A small pilot measured like the baseline shows whether the fix really works.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Control the gain, and plan your Yellow Belt exam
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Set up a control check for the fix and make a dated study-and-test plan.
This lesson builds toward: Given a root cause, you will choose a fix that removes waste or mistakes, test it on a small scale and set up a control check, with data before and after the fix. Using the official ASQ or IASSC page, you will make a dated study-and-test plan for a Yellow Belt exam, with the exam format and rules checked on that page.
Many fixes fade when people slip back into old habits. In the Control step you keep the gain: write the new way as standard work (a short checklist or picture of the right steps), train people on it, and keep measuring. A run chart plots your numbers over time with a center line; a control chart adds limits that show when the process has changed more than normal. Write a simple control plan: what to check, how often, who checks, and what to do if the number gets worse.
Now plan your credential. The ASQ Certified Six Sigma Yellow Belt has no experience or education requirement, and its exams are open book with your own bound reference materials, according to asq.org. The IASSC Certified Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt has no prerequisites, and its exam is closed book and proctored, according to iassc.org. Formats, fees and rules change, so read the official page before you register. Some employers also run their own in-house Yellow Belt training.
Download the certifying body's Body of Knowledge (the list of topics the exam can cover), mark each topic you know, and plan study time for the rest. Put real dates on the calendar and book the exam only when your practice scores are steady.
Step by step:
- Write the new way as standard work.
- Make a control plan: what, how often, who, and what to do if it gets worse.
- Keep a run chart going for at least a few weeks.
- Choose an exam and read its official page.
- Use the Body of Knowledge to plan study dates and a target test date.
Words to know:
- Standard work: the agreed best way to do a task, written as simple steps or pictures.
- Run chart: a line chart of a measure over time, used to see trends.
- Control chart: a run chart with limits that show when a process changes more than normal.
- Control plan: a short plan saying what to check, how often, who checks and what to do if it slips.
- Body of Knowledge: the official list of topics an exam can cover.
Official sources:
- ASQ: Certified Six Sigma Yellow Belt (requirements, exam and Body of Knowledge)
- IASSC: Certified Lean Six Sigma Yellow Belt (ICYB)
Try it now: Final task: finish your one-page project (problem statement and goal, process map, check sheet and defect rate, Pareto chart and 5 Whys, the fix you piloted with before and after numbers, and a control plan). Then open the ASQ or IASSC Yellow Belt page, write the exam format you found there, and make a study plan with at least four dated study sessions and a target test date.
You can now keep a gain with standard work and a control plan, and follow a dated plan toward a Yellow Belt exam.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Problem and goal The statement is vague or names a cause or solution; the goal has no number or date. The statement gives what, where, since when and how big; the goal has a number and a date; a process map of 5 to 8 steps is included. Also includes a SIPOC or names what the customer cares about most (CTQ). Data and defect rate Fewer than 20 data points, or no clear definition of a defect. A check sheet with at least 20 data points and the defect rate with the math shown. Also gives DPMO, or shows the same counting rules were used every day. Root cause No Pareto chart, or the 5 Whys ends in blame. A Pareto chart sorted biggest to smallest and a 5 Whys that ends in a process cause someone can act on. Also uses a fishbone to show other causes the team ruled out. Fix and control The fix was not tested, or there are no before and after numbers. A piloted fix with before and after numbers and a control plan (what, how often, who, what if it slips). Also includes standard work or a run chart covering several weeks. DMAIC story The page jumps around and the steps are missing or out of order. The page follows Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control in order. The learner can explain the project in under two minutes, as in a job interview. Study-and-test plan No dates, or no official page checked. Names an exam, the format checked on its official page, at least four dated study sessions and a target test date. Also maps study sessions to Body of Knowledge topics and includes practice-test dates. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Three months after a fix, errors are creeping back up. Which step was missing?
check.why: Control keeps the gain with standard work, training and ongoing checks.

check.q: Where should you check the current rules and format of a Yellow Belt exam?
options: A friend who passed years ago
An ad for a cheap course
The certifying body's official page, such as asq.org or iassc.org
check.why: Exam rules, formats and fees change; the certifying body's own page is the source to trust.
